apis.name: underscore
apis.pseudocode:
underscore(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = empty byte buffer
    for i in 0 .. len(input)-1:
        c = input[i]
        if c >= 0x41 ('A') and c <= 0x5A ('Z'):
            if i > 0:
                out.push(0x5F '_')          # PURELY POSITIONAL test on the index i,
                                            # NOT "previous byte was not '_'" and NOT
                                            # "previous byte was lowercase/alnum".
            out.push(c + 0x20)              # ASCII tolower
        else:
            out.push(c)                     # every other byte copied verbatim
    return out

NOTES (all observed):
  * Only bytes 0x41..0x5A are treated as uppercase. Bytes >= 0x80 (Latin-1 / UTF-8
    continuation & lead bytes) are NEVER lowercased and NEVER trigger a '_'.
    (C locale confirmed by exhaustive sweep of bytes 0x01..0xFF.)
  * NO de-duplication of '_': an existing '_' before an uppercase letter still gets
    another '_' inserted.
  * '-' is NEVER converted to '_'.  ' ', '\t', '.', '/', ':' etc. are all left alone.
  * '::' is NOT converted to '/' (unlike Rails' ActiveSupport underscore).
  * Digits are not special: a digit before an uppercase letter still gets a '_'
    inserted, and an uppercase letter before a digit does not.
  * Output length is between len(input) and 2*len(input).
  * Byte-based, not char-based: a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence followed by an ASCII
    uppercase letter gets '_' inserted between them.

edge_cases: Empty input is untestable: the program aborts (std::out_of_range from substr in line 18 demodulize) before any stdout is flushed. Logically the loop body never runs, so underscore("") == "".
Single uppercase letter gets NO leading underscore: "A" -> "a", "X" -> "x" (the i>0 guard).

The i>0 guard is strictly positional. "_A" -> "__a" and "a_B" -> "a__b" prove there is no "skip if previous byte is already '_'" de-duplication, and "-A" -> "-_a" proves '-' does not suppress insertion either.
'-' is never rewritten to '_': "kebab-case" -> "kebab-case", "a-B" -> "a-_b".
'::' is preserved literally, NOT turned into '/': "Foo::Bar" -> "foo::_bar".
Consecutive uppercase runs are fully exploded, one '_' per letter (no acronym handling): "HTMLParser" -> "h_t_m_l_parser", "URLValue" -> "u_r_l_value".
Digits are ordinary: "9A" -> "9_a" (underscore inserted after a digit), "A9" -> "a9" (none before a digit).
Whitespace is preserved verbatim and does not suppress the underscore: "Hello World" -> "hello _world" (note the space AND the underscore), "a\tB" -> "a\t_b", "  A" -> "  _a".
Bytes >= 0x80 are inert: never case-folded, never trigger '_' themselves, but DO count as a position so a following ASCII uppercase gets '_' ("\xc3\xa9A" -> "\xc3\xa9_a").
Multi-byte UTF-8 uppercase letters (É U+00C9, Ω U+03A9) come out unchanged — confirms C locale / ASCII-only toupper-tolower.
Control bytes 0x01..0x1F (incl. LF 0x0A, CR 0x0D, VT 0x0B, FF 0x0C) and DEL 0x7F are copied verbatim and count as positions.
NUL (0x00) is not testable through argv.

Any input whose LAST byte is ':' makes the whole program abort (line 18 demodulize does substr past the end), so line 5 is not directly observable for those; ':' in every other position behaves as an ordinary byte.
Output can be up to 2x the input length (all-uppercase input), so pre-allocate 2*len.

apis.name: dasherize
apis.pseudocode:
dasherize(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = copy of input
    for i in 0 .. len(out)-1:
        if out[i] == 0x5F ('_'):
            out[i] = 0x2D ('-')
    return out

That is the ENTIRE operation: a 1:1 in-place byte substitution of '_' -> '-'.
Explicitly verified to do NOTHING else:
  * length is always exactly preserved (no insertions, no deletions)
  * case is NOT changed ("A_B" -> "A-B", "Hello_World" -> "Hello-World")
  * spaces / tabs / newlines / other punctuation are untouched ("a b" -> "a b")
  * pre-existing '-' bytes are left alone, NOT collapsed or de-duplicated
    ("a__b" -> "a--b", "_-_" -> "---")
  * leading and trailing '_' are converted like any other ("_leading" -> "-leading",
    "trailing_" -> "trailing-")
  * bytes >= 0x80 pass through untouched; the substitution is byte-wise so it can
    never corrupt a UTF-8 sequence (0x5F never appears inside a multi-byte sequence)

apis.name: parameterize
apis.pseudocode:
parameterize(input: bytes) -> bytes

STEP 1 - per-byte map (no lookahead, no state, purely positional):
  out = []
  for each byte b in input:
      if b in 0x30..=0x39 ('0'..'9'):   out.push(b)            # digits kept as-is
      elif b in 0x61..=0x7A ('a'..'z'): out.push(b)            # lowercase kept as-is
      elif b in 0x41..=0x5A ('A'..'Z'): out.push(b + 0x20)     # uppercase -> lowercase, ASCII only
      elif b == 0x20 (SPACE):           out.push(0x2D '-')     # ONLY the space byte becomes '-'
      else:                             DROP b (emit nothing)

  CORRECTION TO THE STATED HYPOTHESIS: it is NOT isspace().
  Only 0x20 maps to '-'. The other C-locale whitespace bytes 0x09 \t, 0x0A \n,
  0x0B \v, 0x0C \f, 0x0D \r are DROPPED exactly like punctuation.
  Verified by exhaustive sweep of every byte 0x01..0xFF.
  Also dropped: '-' (0x2D) and '_' (0x5F) in the INPUT, all ASCII punctuation,
  all control bytes, 0x7F, and every high byte 0x80..=0xFF (so UTF-8 multi-byte
  sequences vanish entirely, byte by byte - no case folding, no substitution).

STEP 2 - trim '-' from BOTH ends, unbounded, no squeezing:
  start = index of first byte in out that is != '-'   (out.find_first_not_of('-'))
  if no such byte exists:  return ""                  (out was empty or all '-')
  end   = index of last  byte in out that is != '-'   (out.find_last_not_of('-'))
  return out[start ..= end]

  Trimming removes ALL leading and ALL trailing '-' (verified with 10 leading /
  10 trailing spaces), NOT just one. Internal runs of '-' are NEVER squeezed:
  N consecutive spaces in the interior produce exactly N '-' (verified N=1..8).
  The trim operates on the MAPPED RESULT, not on the raw input: input
  ' . a' (space, dot, space, 'a') maps to '--a' and trims to 'a'; if the code had
  instead trimmed input whitespace first it would have produced '-a'.

Output is always pure ASCII [a-z0-9-], can never contain a newline, and can be empty.

LINE 12 is exactly parameterize("A " + word + " Test") - same function, no special
casing. It is an oracle when line 11 is empty: the surrounding "A " and " Test"
prevent the interior '-' from being trimmed, so the interior dash count is visible.
For a word that is k spaces and nothing else, line 12 = 'a' + (k+2) dashes + 'test'.

edge_cases: ONLY byte 0x20 becomes '-'. \t (0x09), \n (0x0A), \v (0x0B), \f (0x0C), \r (0x0D) are DROPPED, not converted. This contradicts the 'isspace -> dash' hypothesis and is the single most important correction.
'-' (0x2D) and '_' (0x5F) present in the INPUT are dropped, not treated as separators: 'a-b' -> 'ab', 'a__b' -> 'ab', 'Hello-World' -> 'helloworld'.
Internal runs are NEVER squeezed: 'a  b' -> 'a--b', 'a        b' -> 'a' + 8 dashes + 'b'. Only the two ends are trimmed.
Trimming is unbounded on both ends: 10 leading spaces and 10 trailing spaces both collapse to nothing.
Trimming acts on the MAPPED output, not on input whitespace. ' . a' -> 'a' (mapped '--a'), not '-a'. Equivalent to find_first_not_of('-') / find_last_not_of('-') + substr.

An input that maps entirely to '-' or to nothing yields the empty string: '---', '...', '  ', ' ', '-', '_', '.', UTF-8 accents, CJK, 0x7F bytes all -> '' on line 11. Line 12 still reveals the interior dash count.
All bytes 0x80..=0xFF are dropped - no case mapping, no substitution. UTF-8 is destroyed byte-by-byte: 'héllo wörld' -> 'hllo-wrld', 'café' -> 'caf', 'naïve' -> 'nave'.
Digits 0-9 preserved verbatim; A-Z lowered by +0x20; a-z unchanged. Nothing else survives.
Output alphabet is strictly [a-z0-9-]; it can never contain whitespace, a newline, or a non-ASCII byte, and it never starts or ends with '-'.

Line 12 = parameterize("A " + word + " Test") with no special handling. Because 'A' and 'Test' anchor both ends, the trim never eats the joining dashes, so line 12 exposes the pre-trim interior for inputs whose line 11 is empty.
Line 12 dash arithmetic: for a word that is k spaces and nothing else, line 12 = 'a' + (k+2) dashes + 'test' (verified k=0 via '.', k=1, k=2, k=3).

Empty word aborts the whole program before any output (std::out_of_range from demodulize on line 18), so parameterize('') is not directly observable; ' ', '.', '-' confirm the empty-result path instead.
Unrelated crash to avoid during fuzzing: any word ending in ':' aborts the binary via demodulize, wiping all 20 lines. Filter those inputs when differential-testing parameterize.

uncertainties: Byte 0x00 cannot be passed through argv, so its behavior is untestable from the CLI. By analogy with every other control byte (0x01-0x1F all dropped) it would almost certainly be dropped, but this is inference, not observation.

I cannot distinguish an implementation that trims with a repeated pop/erase loop from one that uses find_first_not_of('-')/find_last_not_of('-')+substr - they are behaviorally identical for every input. The Rust sketch uses the position/rposition form, which matches all probes.

I cannot rule out a 'trim-then-map' variant that happens to coincide, but ' . a' -> 'a' and 'a . ' -> 'a' definitively rule out any variant that trims the raw input's whitespace before mapping, which was the only plausible alternative.

parameterize on a truly empty string is not directly observable because the harness aborts in demodulize before printing. Line 12 for words that map to nothing ('.', '-', '_') is consistent with parameterize('') returning '', so the empty-input path is inferred rather than directly observed.

The exhaustive byte sweep used the fixed context 'a' + byte + 'b'. A hypothetical position-dependent rule (e.g. a byte behaving differently at index 0) is not excluded by that sweep alone, though 1000 randomized differential probes with varied positions and lengths found zero disagreements, making any such rule very unlikely.

apis.name: camelize(word)  [line 3, default 2nd param — lower-camel]
apis.pseudocode:
camelize_lower(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = []
    cap = false
    for c in input:                     # iterate raw bytes, no UTF-8 decoding
        if c == 0x5F ('_'):
            cap = true                  # underscore is CONSUMED, never emitted
                                        # (repeated underscores just keep cap = true)
        else if cap:
            out.push(ascii_toupper(c))  # only 'a'..'z' (0x61..0x7A) map to c-32; every
                                        # other byte (digits, punctuation, control,
                                        # 0x80..0xFF) is pushed unchanged
            cap = false
        else:
            out.push(c)
    return out

# NOTES CONFIRMED BY PROBE:
#  - cap starts FALSE, so the very first byte of the input is emitted verbatim
#    UNLESS the input begins with '_' (then the first surviving byte is uppercased).
#  - The first byte is NEVER lowercased. "Hello_world" -> "HelloWorld",
#    "HELLO_WORLD" -> "HELLOWORLD", "X_y_Z" -> "XYZ".
#  - A trailing '_' leaves cap = true with nothing following; it is simply dropped.
#  - No other separator is special: '-', ' ', '.', '/', ':', tab, high bytes all pass through.
#  - '/' is NOT converted to '::' (unlike Rails).
#  - An all-underscore input yields the empty string (no crash).
#  - No acronym table, no inflection rules, no locale involvement.

Trailing '_': "ab_" -> "ab" — dangling cap flag is discarded, no crash.

Underscore before a UTF-8 lead byte: "a_\xc3\xa9x" -> "a\xc3\xa9x". The cap is consumed by 0xC3 which toupper leaves alone, so the multi-byte char is neither uppercased nor corrupted. Byte-based, not char-based.

Line 3 NEVER lowercases anything: "Hello_world"->"HelloWorld", "HELLO_WORLD"->"HELLOWORLD", "HelloWorld"->"HelloWorld". It is purely 'remove underscores, uppercase the byte after each run of underscores'.
'/' is NOT translated to '::' (Rails does this): "foo_bar/baz_qux" -> "fooBar/bazQux".
Existing "::" passes through untouched: "Foo::Bar" -> "Foo::Bar".
No acronym/inflection table is consulted; output is a pure character transform.

Single-byte input ':' (and "_:") makes the whole program abort with std::out_of_range from demodulize (line 18) before stdout is flushed, so lines 3/4 are unobservable for those inputs — this is a line-18 property, not a camelize property.

#    promoted); "-a" -> "-a"; " a" -> " a"; "helloWorld" -> "HelloWorld"
#    (the rest of the string is NOT lowercased).
#  - Empty result (e.g. input "_", "__", "___") -> empty output, no crash,

apis.name: humanize
apis.pseudocode:
humanize(input: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>

1. out = copy of input bytes (same length, always).
2. for i in 0..out.len():
       if out[i] == 0x5F ('_') { out[i] = 0x20 (' ') }
3. if out.len() > 0:
       out[0] = ascii_toupper(out[0])
   where ascii_toupper(b) = if 0x61 <= b <= 0x7A { b - 32 } else { b }
4. return out

NOTHING ELSE HAPPENS. Explicitly verified NOT done:
  - no stripping of a trailing "_id" (Rails behavior is ABSENT): "user_id" -> "User id", "id" -> "Id", "_id" -> " id".
  - no lowercasing of the remainder: "aB" -> "AB", "HELLO WORLD" -> "HELLO WORLD", "AuthorID" -> "AuthorID".
  - no squeezing of runs of '_' : "a__b" -> "A  b" (two spaces), "a___b" -> "A   b".
  - no trimming of leading/trailing whitespace or underscores: "  spaced  " -> "  spaced  " (bytes 20 20 73 70 61 63 65 64 20 20), "a_" -> "A " (41 20), "_a" -> " a" (20 61).
  - '-' is NOT converted: "hello-world" -> "Hello-world".
  - only byte index 0 is uppercased, even when that byte is a space produced by the '_' replacement or already a space: "_a" -> " a" (the 'a' stays lowercase), " a" -> " a".

apis.name: titleize
apis.pseudocode:
titleize(input: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>

1. out = empty byte vector
2. cap_next = true
3. for each byte c in input (in order):
       if c == 0x20 (' '):
           push 0x20 into out
           cap_next = true
       else if cap_next:
           push ascii_toupper(c) into out
           cap_next = false
       else:
           push ascii_tolower(c) into out
4. return out

where ascii_toupper(b) = if 0x61 <= b <= 0x7A { b - 32 } else { b }
      ascii_tolower(b) = if 0x41 <= b <= 0x5A { b + 32 } else { b }

CRITICAL: the ONLY word separator is the literal byte 0x20 (space).
  - '_' is NOT a separator and is NOT converted to a space (no underscore()/humanize()
    pre-pass): "hello_world" -> "Hello_world", "a_b_c" -> "A_b_c", "_a_b_" -> "_a_b_".
  - '-' is NOT a separator: "hello-world" -> "Hello-world" (the 'w' is lowercased, not capped).
  - '\t' (09), '\r' (0D), '\v' (0B), '\f' (0C), '\n' (0A) are NOT separators:
    "a\tb" -> "A\tb" (the 'b' stays lowercase).
  - '.' and ':' are NOT separators: "a.b c.d" -> "A.b C.d", "Foo::Bar" -> "Foo::bar".

CRITICAL: cap_next is consumed by ANY non-space byte, even one that toupper cannot
change (digit, punctuation, byte >= 0x80). It is NOT "skip until a letter":
  - "a 1b" -> "A 1b"  (the '1' consumes cap_next, so 'b' is lowercased)
  - hex c3 a9 20 78 ("e-acute x") -> hex c3 a9 20 58: the c3 consumes cap_next
    (unchanged), a9 is lowercased (unchanged), then 'x' after the space -> 'X'.

Every non-first-of-word byte is LOWERCASED (this is a full re-case, not a
capitalize-only pass): "HelloWorld" -> "Helloworld", "HELLO WORLD" -> "Hello World",
"AuthorID" -> "Authorid", "McDonald" -> "Mcdonald".

A space always emits a space and re-arms cap_next; runs of spaces are preserved
verbatim and are not squeezed or trimmed: "  spaced  " (20 20 73 70 61 63 65 64 20 20)
-> "  Spaced  " (20 20 53 70 61 63 65 64 20 20). Output length always equals input length.

apis.name: truncate(word, 5)
apis.pseudocode:
truncate(s: &[u8], len: usize = 5, omission: &[u8] = b"...") -> Vec<u8>

  // Pure BYTE operation. No UTF-8 awareness, no word/whitespace boundary logic,
  // no trimming. Never throws for any observed input.

  1. if s.len() <= len:            // threshold is <=, i.e. 5 bytes passes through, 6 truncates
         return s.to_vec()         // exact copy, including trailing spaces/tabs/high bytes
  2. keep = len - omission.len()   // = 5 - 3 = 2 for the call under test
  3. return s[0 .. keep] ++ omission   // ALWAYS exactly 5 bytes: first 2 bytes of s, then 0x2E 0x2E 0x2E

  Consequences observed:
   - For every s with s.len() >= 6 the output is byte-identical to s[0..2] + "..." (5 bytes total),
     independent of s.len() (verified up to 300 bytes).
   - s[0..2] is a raw byte slice: it WILL cut a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence in half, emitting a
     lone lead byte (0xC3, 0xF0) or a lone continuation byte with no replacement/validation.
   - Whitespace is data: "      " (6 spaces) -> "  ..."; "hello world" -> "he...".

evidence.output: abcde   (od: a b c d e \n) -- threshold is <= 5, NOT < 5
od: 303 251 303 251 a \n  -- unchanged, so the limit is BYTES not characters
od: 303 251 . . . \n  -- 4 chars of input would fit a char-based limit; it truncated, confirming byte length

evidence.input: $'a\xc3\xa9\xc3\xa9\xc3\xa9' (7 bytes: 61 c3 a9 c3 a9 c3 a9)
evidence.output: od: a 303 . . . \n  -- MID-SEQUENCE SPLIT: emits lone lead byte 0xC3 with no continuation. Output is invalid UTF-8.
od: 360 237 . . . \n  -- first 2 bytes of a 4-byte sequence
od: (space) a . . . \n  -- no trimming; leading space is byte 0

evidence.input: 'ab cd ' (6 bytes, trailing space at index 5)
evidence.output: ab...   -- trailing whitespace still counts toward the length

edge_cases: Threshold is inclusive: size() <= 5 returns the input verbatim; size() >= 6 always returns exactly 5 bytes. Verified for every length 1..20 and at 300.
Length is measured in BYTES (std::string::size()), not characters. A 3-character/6-byte UTF-8 string IS truncated; a 3-character/5-byte one is NOT.

The prefix slice can split a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, producing invalid UTF-8 (e.g. 61 C3 2E 2E 2E). A Rust port must operate on Vec<u8>; `&s[..2]` on a &str would panic on a char boundary where the C++ happily cuts.
No whitespace trimming, no word/separator boundary snapping, no ellipsis character (U+2026) - the omission is three ASCII 0x2E bytes.
Bytes >= 0x80 are treated as ordinary data bytes and are copied unchanged.
Never throws. Empty input would return empty, but the empty word cannot be observed here because line 18 aborts the process first (see demodulize).
Output for any input of length >= 6 is exactly 5 bytes, so the line length is a reliable oracle.

apis.name: demodulize("Test::" + word)
apis.pseudocode:
demodulize(s: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>   // may throw std::out_of_range

  // SURVIVING HYPOTHESIS = (A):  pos = s.find_last_of(':');  return s.substr(pos + 2)
  // Hypothesis (B) (pos = s.rfind("::"); substr(pos+3)) is FALSIFIED - see evidence.
  // The bug in the original: it locates the last ':' CHARACTER but then advances by the
  // length of the "::" SEPARATOR, so it always eats one extra byte.

  1. pos = index of the LAST byte in s equal to 0x3A (':'); npos if none
  2. if pos == npos:  return s.to_vec()        // <-- unreachable via line 18, see uncertainties
  3. start = pos + 2
  4. if start > s.len():  throw std::out_of_range(
         "basic_string::substr: __pos (which is {start}) > this->size() (which is {s.len()})")
     // note: start == s.len() is LEGAL and yields the empty string
  5. return s[start ..].to_vec()

  ---- Specialised to line 18, where s = "Test::" ++ word (so s.len() == 6 + word.len()) ----
  The literal prefix always supplies colons at s[4] and s[5], so pos >= 5 and the npos
  branch never fires. Let m = word.len().

  * m == 0                          -> pos = 5, start = 7 > 6  => ABORT
                                       (exact message: __pos (which is 7) > this->size() (which is 6))
  * word contains no ':' (m >= 1)   -> pos = 5, start = 7 <= 6+m  => result = word[1..]
                                       i.e. the word with its FIRST BYTE dropped ('cat' -> 'at')
  * word contains ':' at last index j:
      pos = 6 + j, start = 8 + j
      - if j == m-1 (word ENDS with ':')  -> start = m+7 > m+6  => ABORT
                                             (message: __pos (which is m+7) > size (which is m+6))
      - else                              -> result = word[j+2 ..]
                                             (empty when j == m-2, i.e. exactly one byte follows)

  ==> ABORT (SIGABRT, nothing on stdout, exit 134) IFF word.is_empty() OR word ends with 0x3A.
      Otherwise the line is word[k..] where k = (last ':' index in word) + 2, or 1 if no ':'.

  All slicing is BYTE slicing; it will emit a bare UTF-8 continuation byte.

edge_cases: ABORT CONDITION (exact): line 18 throws std::out_of_range iff word.is_empty() OR word's last byte is 0x3A (':'). Verified on '', ':', '::', ':::', 'b:', 'x:', 'a::', 'a:b:', 'abc:', 'hello:', $'\xc3\xa9:' plus 401 randomized colon-heavy cases. When it aborts, the process dies with SIGABRT (exit 134) and stdout is EMPTY - lines 1-17 were buffered and never flushed - so a Rust port that panics must also suppress all prior output to match.

The abort message is deterministic and useful as an oracle: "basic_string::substr: __pos (which is {last_colon_index+2}) > this->size() (which is {6+word.len()})". Observed (7,6) for '', (8,7) for ':', (9,8) for 'b:' and '::', (10,9) for ':a:' and ':::'.

start == s.len() is NOT an error for substr - it yields the empty string. This is why 'x', 'a:b', 'abc:d' produce an empty (but present) line rather than aborting. Getting this off-by-one wrong flips output between "" and a panic.
The function drops one byte too many: with no ':' in the word the result is word[1..], so a 1-byte word always yields "". This is a faithful bug, not a transcription error.
The delimiter is the single byte 0x3A only. '.', '/', ';', '|', '\\', '_', '-', '#', '$', space, TAB and every byte 0x80-0xFF were each verified non-delimiting.
Slicing is byte-based and routinely produces invalid UTF-8 (bare continuation bytes 0xA9, 0x9F 0x98 0x80). The port must use Vec<u8>; &str indexing would panic where C++ succeeds.
A word containing a SINGLE colon is the decisive test between find_last_of(':')+2 and rfind("::")+3; ten such probes all matched find_last_of.
Embedded NUL bytes cannot be tested through argv, so behavior on interior 0x00 is unobservable (C++ std::string would handle it, a C-string path would not).

uncertainties: demodulize's npos branch (`if (pos == npos) return s;`) is UNREACHABLE through line 18, because the argument is always "Test::" + word and the literal prefix guarantees colons at indices 4 and 5. So `pos` is always >= 5 and the no-colon path was never exercised by any probe. Returning `s` unchanged is the conventional implementation and is what the surviving hypothesis (A) asserts, but it is NOT backed by an observation here. If another line in the 20 exposes demodulize on a colon-free string, that would settle it; from line 17/18 alone it cannot be.

truncate is only ever called with len = 5, so the internal decomposition `keep = len - omission.len()` (2 = 5 - 3) is inferred, not directly observed. What IS observed is the strictly weaker fact: size() <= 5 -> identity, size() >= 6 -> first 2 bytes + "...". Any formula that yields 2 and "..." at len=5 fits the data equally well. Consequently the behavior for other len values (especially len < 3, where `len - omission.len()` would underflow) is unknown.

Whether truncate accepts an omission/separator parameter with defaults (as ActiveSupport's truncate does) is unobservable; I verified only that no separator/word-boundary snapping happens at len=5 ('hello world' -> 'he...', not 'hello...' or 'h...').

Bytes 0x00 cannot be passed through argv, so neither function was tested with an embedded NUL. If the implementation ever touches a C string internally, a NUL would truncate early; std::string would not. Untestable from this harness.
For truncate I tested lengths 1..20 plus 300. Behavior at extremely large sizes (near allocation limits) was not probed.

Line 18's ABORT kills the whole process, so for any word ending in ':' or the empty word I could observe NO stdout at all - meaning line 17's value for those inputs (e.g. word 'abcdef:') is unobservable even though truncate itself would clearly not throw.

apis.name: pluralize
apis.pseudocode:
pluralize(word: bytes) -> bytes

UNCOUNTABLE = [ "equipment", "information", "rice", "money",
                "species", "series", "fish", "sheep",
                "jeans", "police" ]      // exactly these 10, in this order

1. If word (the WHOLE byte string, no trimming, no lowercasing, no word-boundary
   search) is byte-for-byte EQUAL to any entry of UNCOUNTABLE:
       return word unchanged (a copy).
2. Otherwise:
       return word with the single byte 0x73 ('s') appended.

That is the entire rule. There is NO other transformation:
  - no y->ies      (city -> "citys",  baby -> "babys",  fly -> "flys")
  - no x/ch/ss/sh->es (box -> "boxs", church -> "churchs", class -> "classs", dish -> "dishs")
  - no o->oes      (tomato -> "tomatos", potato -> "potatos", hero -> "heros")
  - no f/fe->ves   (leaf -> "leafs",  knife -> "knifes", wolf -> "wolfs")
  - no is->es      (axis -> "axiss",  analysis -> "analysiss", crisis -> "crisiss")
  - no us->i       (octopus -> "octopuss", virus -> "viruss", cactus -> "cactuss")
  - no um/on->a    (datum -> "datums", medium -> "mediums", criterion -> "criterions")
  - no ix/ex->ices (matrix -> "matrixs", vertex -> "vertexs", index -> "indexs")
  - no ouse->ice   (mouse -> "mouses", louse -> "louses")
  - no bus->buses  (bus -> "buss"),  no quiz->quizzes (quiz -> "quizs")
  - no ox->oxen    (ox -> "oxs")
  - no alias/status->es (alias -> "aliass", status -> "statuss")
  - no (n)ews rule (news -> "newss")
  - no irregular map (man -> "mans", child -> "childs", person -> "persons",
     tooth -> "tooths", foot -> "foots", goose -> "gooses", people -> "peoples")
  - no "already plural -> unchanged" check (boxes -> "boxess", fishes -> "fishess",
     mice -> "mices", children -> "childrens", data -> "datas")

MATCHING DETAILS (all probed):
  - CASE-SENSITIVE: "Sheep" -> "Sheeps", "SHEEP" -> "SHEEPs", "sHeep" -> "sHeeps",
    "ShEeP" -> "ShEePs", "Fish" -> "Fishs", "FISH" -> "FISHs", "Money" -> "Moneys",
    "POLICE" -> "POLICEs", "JEANS" -> "JEANSs", "Equipment" -> "Equipments".
    Only the all-lowercase spelling is uncountable.
  - WHOLE-STRING equality, NOT a suffix/regex/word-boundary match:
    "goldfish" -> "goldfishs", "bluefish" -> "bluefishs", "xfish" -> "xfishs",
    "fishx" -> "fishxs", "gold fish" -> "gold fishs", "a fish" -> "a fishs",
    "gold-fish" -> "gold-fishs", "x_fish" -> "x_fishs", "the police" -> "the polices",
    "blacksheep" -> "blacksheeps", "xseries" -> "xseriess".
  - NO whitespace trimming before compare: "fish " -> "fish s", " fish" -> " fishs".
  - Purely byte-based, locale/encoding agnostic: bytes >= 0x80 pass through and get
    an 's' appended ("caf\xc3\xa9" -> "caf\xc3\xa9s", "\xff" -> "\xffs",
    "\x80\x81" -> "\x80\x81s", "\xe4\xb8\xad\xe6\x96\x87" -> that + "s").
  - Control bytes pass through: "a\tb" -> "a\tbs".
  - Length independent: 100000 'a' bytes -> 100001 bytes ending in 's'.
  - Empty input never reaches a normal return in this program: the harness aborts in
    line 18 (demodulize) with std::out_of_range before any stdout flush, so nothing
    is printed. As a function, pluralize("") would return "s" by the rule above
    (unverifiable in isolation from this binary).

100001 bytes ending in 's' (repetition of an uncountable is NOT uncountable)

A 4+-letter lowercase string that is NOT present anywhere in the binary and NOT in my noun list was not brute-forced (456976 candidates at length 4 alone would take ~24 min). // /workspace/dataset/test20_executable, then fully re-derived byte-wise and validated
// (0 mismatches on 22,358 fuzzed inputs). Matching is BYTE-based and CASE-SENSITIVE
// (all patterns lowercase, no icase flag). `$` = END OF STRING, not end of line.

n = len(b)
if n == 0: return b        // unobservable, see uncertainties

// Step 1: uncountables -- WHOLE-STRING, BYTE-EXACT, CASE-SENSITIVE
UNCOUNTABLE = {equipment, information, rice, money, species, series, fish, sheep, jeans, police}
if b in UNCOUNTABLE: return b

// Step 2: ordered chain, FIRST MATCH WINS, return immediately.
// This order == lexicographic byte order of the 24 regex pattern strings
// (i.e. std::map iteration order), NOT the Rails source order.
// Proof it is not source order: "axes" -> "axis", so R10 beats R22.

ends(b,t) := len(b) >= len(t) && b[len(b)-len(t)..] == t

R1  ((a)naly|(b)a|(d)iagno|(p)arenthe|(p)rogno|(s)ynop|(t)he)ses$ -> $1$2sis
    if ends(b,"ses"):
        rest = b[..n-3]
        for st in [analy, ba, diagno, parenthe, progno, synop, the]:
            if ends(rest, st):
                return rest + ("asis" if st=="analy" else "sis")
        // $1 is re-emitted verbatim so which stem matched cannot change the output;
        // group 2 is "a" only in the analy branch, empty (unparticipating) otherwise.

R2  ([^aeiouy]|qu)ies$ -> $1y
    if ends(b,"ies") && n>=4:
        c = b[n-4]

R3  ([^f])ves$ -> $1fe
    if ends(b,"ves") && n>=4 && b[n-4] != 'f': return b[..n-3] + "fe"

R4  ([lr])ves$ -> $1f            *** UNREACHABLE (R3 fires first) ***
    if ends(b,"ves") && n>=4 && b[n-4] in {l,r}: return b[..n-3] + "f"

apis.name: parameterize
apis.pseudocode:
parameterize(input: bytes) -> bytes

STEP 1 - per-byte map (no lookahead, no state, purely positional):
  out = []
  for each byte b in input:
      if b in 0x30..=0x39 ('0'..'9'):   out.push(b)            # digits kept as-is
      elif b in 0x61..=0x7A ('a'..'z'): out.push(b)            # lowercase kept as-is
      elif b in 0x41..=0x5A ('A'..'Z'): out.push(b + 0x20)     # uppercase -> lowercase, ASCII only
      elif b == 0x20 (SPACE):           out.push(0x2D '-')     # ONLY the space byte becomes '-'
      else:                             DROP b (emit nothing)

  It is NOT isspace(). Only 0x20 maps to '-'. The other C-locale whitespace bytes
  0x09 \t, 0x0A \n, 0x0B \v, 0x0C \f, 0x0D \r are DROPPED exactly like punctuation.
  Verified by exhaustive sweep of every byte 0x01..0xFF in 10 different positional
  contexts (leading, trailing, isolated, tripled, interior, space-adjacent,
  uppercase-adjacent) plus 26,670 two-byte combination probes.
  Also dropped: '-' (0x2D) and '_' (0x5F) in the INPUT, all ASCII punctuation,
  all control bytes, 0x7F, and every high byte 0x80..=0xFF (so UTF-8 multi-byte
  sequences vanish entirely, byte by byte - no case folding, no substitution).

STEP 2 - trim '-' from BOTH ends, unbounded, no squeezing:
  start = index of first byte in out that is != '-'   (out.find_first_not_of('-'))
  if no such byte exists:  return ""                  (out was empty or all '-')
  end   = index of last  byte in out that is != '-'   (out.find_last_not_of('-'))
  return out[start ..= end]

  Trimming removes ALL leading and ALL trailing '-' (verified with up to 60 leading
  and 60 trailing spaces simultaneously), NOT just one. Internal runs of '-' are
  NEVER squeezed: N consecutive interior spaces produce exactly N '-' (verified
  exhaustively for N = 1..60). The trim operates on the MAPPED RESULT, not on the
  raw input: input ' . a' (space, dot, space, 'a') maps to '--a' and trims to 'a';
  if the code had instead trimmed input whitespace first it would have produced '-a'.

  * LOCALE-INVARIANT. The ASCII-only classification is hardcoded, not locale
    driven. Identical output under LC_ALL/LANG = C, POSIX, C.utf8, en_US.utf8,
    de_DE.iso88591, fr_FR.iso88591, ru_RU.koi8r, ja_JP.utf8, and tr_TR.utf8.
    Notably tr_TR does NOT produce Turkish dotless-i behaviour: 'I' -> 'i' always.
  * NO CamelCase splitting / no internal underscore() pass. 'HelloWorld' ->
    'helloworld' (not 'hello-world'), 'XMLHttpRequest' -> 'xmlhttprequest'.
  * NO length limit and no truncation: verified on inputs up to 60,000 bytes.
  * Output is always pure ASCII [a-z0-9-], can never contain a newline or a byte
    >= 0x80, never starts or ends with '-', and can be empty.

apis.name: truncate(word, 5)
apis.pseudocode:
truncate(s: &[u8], len: usize = 5, omission: &[u8] = b"...") -> Vec<u8>

  // Pure BYTE operation. No UTF-8 awareness, no word/whitespace boundary logic,
  // no trimming, no case folding. Never observed to throw.

  1. if s.len() <= len:            // inclusive threshold: 5 bytes passes through, 6 truncates
         return s.to_vec()         // exact copy, including leading/trailing spaces, tabs,
                                   // control bytes (0x01..0x1F, 0x7F) and high bytes (0x80..0xFF)
  2. keep = len - omission.len()   // = 5 - 3 = 2 for the only call ever made
  3. return s[0 .. keep] ++ omission   // ALWAYS exactly 5 bytes: s[0], s[1], 0x2E, 0x2E, 0x2E

  Fully confirmed consequences:
   - For every s with s.len() >= 6 the output is byte-identical to s[0..2] ++ b"...",
     independent of s.len() (verified at every length 1..30, and at 100 / 1000 / 10000 /
     100000 / 60001 bytes).
   - s[0] and s[1] are RAW BYTES, copied verbatim. Exhaustively verified: for all 254 byte
     values X in 0x01..0xFF (excluding 0x0A, handled separately) the 6-byte words
     X."bcdef", "a".X."cdef" and "abcde".X produce X+'b'+"...", 'a'+X+"..." and "ab..."
     respectively -- no byte is special-cased, escaped, case-folded or validated.
   - It WILL cut a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence in half, emitting a lone lead byte (0xC3, 0xF0)
     or a lone continuation byte, with no replacement character and no error.
   - Whitespace is data: b"      " -> b"  ..."; b"    xy" -> b"  ..."; b"hello world" -> b"he...";
     b"a bcdefgh" -> b"a ..." (0x61 0x20 2E 2E 2E) -- the kept prefix is NOT right-trimmed.
   - 0x0A is an ordinary data byte too (it just breaks line-oriented harnesses, see edge cases).

demodulize(s: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8>   // may throw std::out_of_range

  // SURVIVING HYPOTHESIS (A):  pos = s.find_last_of(':');  return s.substr(pos + 2)
  // Falsified alternatives (all re-checked here):
  //   (B) pos = s.rfind("::"); substr(pos+3)   -- FALSIFIED by single-colon words
  //   (F) pos = s.find("::");  substr(pos+3)   -- FALSIFIED by the same words
  //   (E) pos = s.find(':');   substr(pos+2)   -- FALSIFIED by 'cat' -> "at" (E predicts "cat")
  // The bug in the original: it locates the last ':' BYTE but then advances by the length of
  // the "::" SEPARATOR, so it always eats one byte too many.

  1. pos = index of the LAST byte in s equal to 0x3A (':'); npos if none
  2. if pos == npos:  return s.to_vec()        // <-- UNREACHABLE via line 18, see uncertainties
  3. start = pos + 2
  4. if start > s.len():  throw std::out_of_range(
         "basic_string::substr: __pos (which is {start}) > this->size() (which is {s.len()})")
     // start == s.len() is LEGAL and yields the empty string

underscore(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = empty byte buffer
    for i in 0 .. len(input)-1:
        c = input[i]
        if c >= 0x41 ('A') and c <= 0x5A ('Z'):
            if i > 0:
                out.push(0x5F '_')          # PURELY POSITIONAL test on the index i.
                                            # NOT "previous byte was not '_'", NOT
                                            # "previous byte was lowercase/alnum", and
                                            # NOT any modular/truncated index test.
            out.push(c + 0x20)              # ASCII tolower (only 0x41..0x5A)
        else:

dasherize(input: bytes) -> bytes:
    out = copy of input
    for i in 0 .. len(out)-1:
        if out[i] == 0x5F ('_'):
